requirement: CFTP carries basic SMTP mail over STANAG 5066, compressed, from one message server to another, reliably; it replaces HMTP, which had no compression.
The annex is Ed3 Annex F section F.14 unchanged; CFTP is a vendor-defined standard taken from client definitions in earlier non-mandatory editions of Annex F.
notes: Status: main 7.2 marks only A, B, C, D, F and S mandatory, so Annex V binds us because we provide the client (V-0003, V-0004).

requirement: An implementation may provide a CFTP client.
A CFTP client that is provided conforms to the requirements of this annex.
CFTP is not used for formal or high grade military messaging, for example military orders.
reason: a rule for how operators use the service, not for the client's behaviour; the user docs say CFTP is for informal mail

requirement: Formal or high grade military messaging uses ACP 142 as Annex Q specifies.
reason: Annex Q (ACP 142) is not in our profile

requirement: CFTP may be used for informal interpersonal e-mail only.
A CFTP client works within the node model of Figure V-1: mail server, then the CFTP client, then the subnetwork through the SIS.
notes: shall (3). Our client talks to the node only through the SIS client library.

requirement: How the CFTP client deals with the mail server is outside the STANAG. In operation the client (the Delivery Agent) takes mail from an incoming spool, compresses the message with information about it (size, id, recipients) into a file, and sends that file to the destination node or nodes with BFTPv1, which the annex defines itself so as not to depend on Ed3 BFTP.
notes: The spool and mail server side are P10-3 (bridges); P10-1 gives received mail to the application (interp V-0089).

requirement: A CFTP client binds to the subnetwork at SAP 12.
notes: Also Annex F Table F-1, p.F-1.

requirement: CFTP uses the original RCOP PDU (RCOPv1) of Figure V-2, which has no application identifier in its header.

RCOPv1 PDU layout (Figure V-2): octet 0 carries the connection ID number in bits 7 to 4 and reserved bits 3 to 0; octet 1 is the U_PDU ID number; octets 2 and 3 are the U_PDU segment number, most significant octet first; the data follow from octet 4.
notes: Kind rcop1 (corpus-format.md 3.10). Figure checked on the rendered page.

requirement: The connection ID number is a value from 0 to 15.
Connection ID number 0 is reserved for non-multiplexed connections.
The reserved bits of an RCOPv1 PDU are set to 0.
U_PDU ID numbers are assigned consecutively to U_PDUs, that is to files.
notes: Item 3. Start value and scope: interp V-0080.

requirement: U_PDU segment numbers are assigned consecutively to the segments of one U_PDU.
The first segment sent of a U_PDU has segment number 0.
A U_PDU that is not segmented goes as one segment numbered 0.
Compressed files go from one CFTP client to another with the Edition 1 Basic File Transfer Protocol (BFTPv1) of the following subsections.
Client delivery confirmation is given by the CFTP Message Acknowledgement (V.4.3) carried as the body of the PDU.

Up to 256 files could be in transfer at once, one per U_PDU ID, acknowledgements being matched to files by U_PDU ID. There is no negotiation of this, so a sender needs prior knowledge that the receiver supports concurrent files.
notes: The prior knowledge sentence is phrased 'must'.

requirement: Delivery confirmation is nominally stop-and-wait: a new file is not sent with a given U_PDU ID until a message acknowledgement has come.
The stop-and-wait recommendation may be relaxed to send files concurrently when the sender knows the receiver supports it.
A new CFTP implementation supports concurrent delivery of several files.
notes: Our receiver keeps files apart by source, connection ID and U_PDU ID (interp V-0088).

requirement: A BFTPv1 PDU has the format of Figure V-3: a header part, then the file data.
A BFTPv1 PDU has the detailed structure of Figure V-4, starting with two synchronisation bytes, DLE then STX.

BFTPv1 fields: the header part is SYNCHRONIZATION (two octets), SIZE_OF_FILENAME (one octet), FILE_NAME (as long as SIZE_OF_FILENAME says) and SIZE_OF_FILE (four octets); the body part is FILE_DATA, as long as SIZE_OF_FILE says.

Figure V-4 draws the BFTPv1 PDU as the RCOPv1 body: octet 0 is 0x10, octet 1 is 0x02, octet 2 is SIZE_OF_FILENAME n, octets 3 to 2 + n the file name, octets 3 + n to 6 + n SIZE_OF_FILE p most significant first, then p octets of file data from octet 7 + n.
notes: Kind bftp1 (corpus-format.md 3.10). Figure checked on the rendered page.

requirement: SIZE_OF_FILENAME is a fixed one-octet field.
The value of SIZE_OF_FILENAME equals the number of octets of the FILENAME field.
notes: shall (2). So a file name is 0 to 255 octets.

requirement: FILENAME is a variable-length field.
The size of FILENAME is given by SIZE_OF_FILENAME.
The first byte of the file name goes in the first byte of FILENAME and the rest follow in order.
File name meaning and naming conventions are outside the STANAG; a file name need not end with a null.
notes: Our choice of name: interp V-0084.

requirement: SIZE_OF_FILE is a fixed four-octet field.
notes: shall (1). So a file is at most 2^32 - 1 octets; our limit is interp V-0087.

requirement: The value of SIZE_OF_FILE is the size in octets of the file sent.
SIZE_OF_FILE is sent highest-order octet first, lowest-order last.
A BFTPv1 PDU larger than the RCOPv1 data field allows (the MTU less 4 octets) is segmented, its successive segments carried in RCOPv1 PDUs with consecutive numbers.
notes: Unnumbered shall. Which number is consecutive: interp V-0071. MTU: interp V-0072.

requirement: A receiving client reassembles a BFTPv1 PDU it finds was segmented.
notes: Marked shall (2). End of the PDU: interp V-0073.

requirement: Subject to local file naming conventions, a receiving client stores the received file under the name sent in its header.
notes: Marked shall (2), like the row above. Interp V-0084.

requirement: So a file may not be stored at the destination under the name it was sent with.
Client delivery confirmation uses the Message Acknowledgement, sent as the body of a CFTP (RCOPv1) PDU.
The Message Acknowledgement (Figure V-5) is two octets, 0x10 then 0x0B, as the RCOPv1 body.

On receiving the last byte of a message, the receiving client sends the Message Acknowledgement with the U_PDU ID and connection ID of the message it acknowledges, to confirm the whole message arrived.
notes: shall (2). Likened to ZMODEM's ZEOF. Interp V-0073, V-0077, V-0079.

requirement: The compressed file is made and decompressed according to RFCs 1950, 1951 and 1952, that is gzip as RFC 1952 defines it.
The data that are compressed are a series of fields separated by the line feed character 0x0A, in the order of Table V-1.
notes: Kind cftp_mail (corpus-format.md 3.10). No line feed follows the last field (V.7 step 3).

requirement: Table V-1 field 1, MessageID: an arbitrary string identifying the message, unique per message and not the Message-ID header; the root file name of the decompressed parts; under 256 characters, upper and lower case letters and digits.
notes: The table cell is cut short in the text extraction; V.7 repeats it (V-0053 to V-0056).

requirement: Table V-1 field 2, RecipientList: the mail addresses taken from the message, separated by commas (0x2C), the first being the Return-Path; with no return path (a bounce) the first address is empty, a single space or nothing, followed by a comma.
notes: V.7 repeats it as shall (V-0057 to V-0060).

requirement: Table V-1 field 3, MessageSize: the size in octets of the Message field that follows, as a decimal number in characters.

Table V-1 field 4, Message: the message as an SMTP receiver gets it, including the terminating CR LF . CR LF and any transparency characters. Notes: every character is 8 bits; the terminator is the five octets 0x0D 0x0A 0x2E 0x0D 0x0A (RFC 821).
Steps 1 and 2: a mail client sends to an SMTP server, and the CFTP application takes the message from the directory the server put it in (Figure V-6 is an example).
The MessageID field is a character string.
The MessageID is unique to one mail message, and is not the ID after 'Message-ID:' in the message header.
When the compressed file is decompressed, the MessageID is the root file name of the decompressed parts.
The MessageID is under 256 characters and may be made of upper and lower case letters and digits.
The RecipientList is a character string of the mail addresses taken from the message, separated by commas (0x2C).
notes: Step 3, shall (1). The extraction drops some words of this sentence; the meaning matches Table V-1.

requirement: The first address in the RecipientList is the Return-Path.
With no return path (for example a bounce from a mail transfer agent) the first address is an empty string, a single space (0x20) or nothing, followed by a comma (0x2C).
The RecipientList is under 10240 characters.
MessageSize is a decimal number in characters ended by a line feed, giving the size in octets of the Message field that follows.
The Message field holds the mail message body part or parts taken from the SMTP envelope.
notes: Step 3, unnumbered shall. Interp V-0083 reads it with Table V-1.

requirement: The CFTP message, header fields included, is compressed according to RFCs 1950, 1951 and 1952, for example with gzip.
The compressed CFTP message is carried in a BFTPv1 PDU, behind a BFTPv1 header, byte aligned in FILE_DATA.
The BFTPv1 PDU is segmented when needed.
Each BFTPv1 segment gets an RCOPv1 header.
notes: Step 7. The text points to Ed3 Annex F.14.3; in Ed4 that header is Figure V-2.

requirement: Each RCOPv1 packet goes in an S_UNIDATA_REQUEST and is sent in a soft link data exchange.
On reception the BFTPv1 message is reassembled when needed, decompressed by an RFC 1952 method, and the CFTP message rebuilt.
Received mail is forwarded to an SMTP server in a standard SMTP dialogue, using the CFTP header for the envelope and the Message field as the payload.
notes: Step 10. Deferred to P10-3 (bridges); P10-1 gives the application the envelope and the message (interp V-0089).

requirement: Figure V-6 is an example message in the right form; it ends with the CR LF . CR LF terminator.

Contradiction: V.4.2 says the segments of a BFTPv1 PDU go with consecutive U_PDU sequence numbers, while V.4 items 3 and 4 give each file one U_PDU ID and number its segments consecutively from 0. Reading: every segment of one BFTPv1 PDU carries the file's U_PDU ID and segment numbers 0, 1, 2 and so on.

Which MTU, and how full the segments are, is NOT STATED. Reading: the MTU is the one S_BIND_ACCEPTED gave; every RCOPv1 PDU is at most the MTU, so carries at most MTU - 4 octets of the BFTPv1 PDU; a sender fills every segment but the last; a receiver does not assume equal segments.
notes: V-0039. SIS MTU: Annex S, S_BIND_ACCEPTED.

requirement: How a receiver knows it has the last segment is NOT STATED: there is no last-segment flag. Reading: the BFTPv1 header gives the PDU length (7 + n + p octets); the PDU is complete when the segments numbered 0 upwards without a gap hold that many octets. Octets beyond the end are ignored.

The delivery mode and priority of CFTP U_PDUs are NOT STATED beyond an S_UNIDATA_REQUEST in a soft link data exchange (step 8). Reading: bind SAP 12 for ARQ; send every U_PDU ARQ, in order, to one node; data segments ask for node delivery confirmation, so a rejected segment is known at once; acknowledgements ask for none. Priority 4, the Annex F default for CFTP [Ed4 F.3 Table F-2, p.F-2]. A group or broadcast destination is refused, since a file needs one acknowledging peer.
notes: V-0067. Annex Q's RCOP also runs over the ARQ service [Ed4 Q.5, p.Q-4].

requirement: The segment number of a Message Acknowledgement is NOT STATED. Reading: 0. A received U_PDU is an acknowledgement when its segment number is 0 and its data are exactly 0x10 0x0B; anything else is a file segment (segment 0 of a file always starts 0x10 0x02).

Timers and retries are NOT STATED. Reading: the sender waits for the acknowledgement for ack_wait (300 s) from the moment the node has confirmed every segment; then it sends the whole file again under the same U_PDU ID. A rejected segment ends the attempt, and the file goes again after retry_delay (60 s). After max_attempts (3) attempts the transfer fails and the application is told. An acknowledgement at any time ends the transfer.
notes: V-0023, V-0045. All three are library options with these defaults.

requirement: Duplicate files are NOT STATED. Reading: the receiver acknowledges every complete file, since a lost acknowledgement makes the sender send again; a complete file identical to the last one completed from the same node with the same connection ID and U_PDU ID is acknowledged again but not delivered twice.
What happens to a file whose segments stop arriving is NOT STATED. Reading: a partly received file is dropped after reassembly_timeout (1 hour) with no new segment for it.

Whether a file that cannot be decompressed or read as a CFTP message is acknowledged is NOT STATED. Reading: the acknowledgement follows the last byte (V.4.3), before any decompression, so such a file is acknowledged (sending it again would bring the same bytes), reported as an error and not delivered.
The first U_PDU ID and its scope are NOT STATED. Reading: one counter per destination node, starting at 0, one up for each new file and wrapping from 255 to 0; a file sent again keeps its ID.

Which connection ID a sender uses is NOT STATED. Reading: 0 (non-multiplexed) for every file. A receiver accepts any connection ID and answers with the one received; reserved bits are ignored on receipt.

V.5 cites RFCs 1950, 1951 and 1952 together and names gzip; step 9 decompresses by RFC 1952. Reading: we send RFC 1952 gzip (one member). A receiver accepts RFC 1952 gzip, one member or more, and, when the data do not start with the gzip magic 0x1F 0x8B, an RFC 1950 zlib stream. Deflate output is not unique, so compressed bytes are compared only after decompression.
notes: V-0046, V-0063, V-0068. Kind cftp_gzip is decode only.

requirement: Table V-1 says the Message field is the message as an SMTP receiver gets it, terminator and transparency included; V.7 says the body parts taken from the SMTP envelope; Figure V-6 shows the terminator. Reading: the field carries the SMTP DATA octets, dot-stuffed (RFC 5321 4.5.2) and ending CR LF . CR LF, and MessageSize counts them. A receiver that finds the terminator removes it and the stuffing; otherwise it takes the field as it is.

The BFTPv1 file name of a CFTP file is NOT STATED. Reading: the sender uses the MessageID. A receiver that stores files makes the name safe locally (any octet other than a letter, digit, '-', '_' or '.' becomes '_', and a name that would be empty or start with '.' gets a prefix), as V.4.2 allows.

MessageID generation and checking: we generate 20 random letters and digits, so under 256 characters and unique in practice. A receiver accepts any MessageID of 1 octet or more with no line feed; an empty MessageID, or a MessageSize that is not a decimal number, makes the file malformed.

RecipientList details: with no return path we write nothing before the first comma; a receiver reads a lone space there as empty. Addresses are taken as written, spaces around them removed on receipt. At least one recipient after the return path is needed, and an empty address after the first makes the list malformed. A sender refuses a list of 10240 characters or more.

Size limit, derived: SIZE_OF_FILE allows 2^32 - 1 octets but the 16-bit segment number allows 65536 segments, so a sender refuses a file whose BFTPv1 PDU needs more than 65536 segments of MTU - 4 octets (about 134 MB at an MTU of 2048).

Concurrency: a sender has one file at a time in transfer to each destination node (V-0023) unless the application says that node takes concurrent files (V-0024, an option, default 1). A receiver always keeps concurrent files apart by source address, connection ID and U_PDU ID (V-0025).

Scope of P10-1: the client library hands received mail (MessageID, return path, recipients and message) to the application and takes mail to send from it. Taking mail from a spool and forwarding to an SMTP server (V.7 steps 2 and 10) are the SMTP bridge of P10-3.
